title: Westbrook Planning Board — Planning Board Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. This was an exceptionally long meeting (nearly 3.5 hours, seven substantive items) with heavy public turnout; summarization necessarily condenses and selects more than usual, especially in the public comment sections. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Chair Larry McWilliams, Vice Chair John Turcotte, Karen Axelson, Jason Frazier, Nancy Litrocapes, Kevin Price, Robin Tannenbaum, Lucas Schrage (alternate). Absent: Oriana Farnham (alternate).

blocks.x: I. Roll Call & Announcements
Roll Call & Agenda Change
Discussion Summary

Chair Larry McWilliams announced that 500 Spring Street, listed on the printed agenda, would instead be heard June 16 because of the heavy workload that night. Roll call: eight of nine seated members were present (McWilliams, Lucas Schrage, Robin Tannenbaum, Kevin Price, Nancy Litrocapes, Jason Frazier, Karen Axelson, and Vice Chair John Turcotte). Oriana Farnham was absent. There were no minutes to approve.
Key Decisions
Quorum established (enough members were present to vote).
Action Items
None.
25-000402 — Site Plan Amendment Extension — 619 Bridgton Rd., Cloutier Properties
Discussion Summary
The applicant, requesting a one-year extension to a previously amended site plan, did not appear. The Chair said the applicant had been contacted about possibly coming to the June 16 meeting.
Key Decisions
Deferred — not reviewed tonight.
Action Items
None.
Regular Business
25-000624 — Site Plan, Subdivision, Village Review — 688–712 Main St., Ryan Le
Discussion Summary
Andy Morrill (BH2M) reported on three issues flagged at a November 2025 review.
First, the sewer was rerouted entirely through the 712 Main Street parcel via a grinder pump.

Second, Building A was pulled back to a 12.5-foot setback (a required distance from a property line) from a shared retaining wall. This removed the need for a maintenance easement (a right to use part of someone else's land) that an abutting neighbor had declined to grant.
Third, stormwater was redesigned with expanded retention and an upstream-watershed bypass.

Abutter Gary Minujian spoke against the project, citing lost backyard privacy and the declined easement request. Staff confirmed that the one-space-per-unit parking meets the City Center District standard.
Vice Chair John Turcotte asked about buffering, given a roughly 40-foot grade difference to abutting yards. A 9-foot retaining wall with a wood guardrail serves as the primary buffer.
Key Decisions
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0 (Robin Tannenbaum recused), moved by John Turcotte, seconded by Kevin Price.
Action Items
None.
25-001113 — Site Plan — 405 Bridgton Rd., Vaughn Dibiase
Discussion Summary

Dustin Roma (DM Roma Consulting Engineers) presented a 7,500-sq-ft, five-bay multi-tenant “service business” building. It has a single access point designed to prevent left turns exiting onto Bridgton Road. It has no outdoor material storage and uses downcast building-mounted lighting. Staff required final plans to commit to whether a sprinkler system will be installed before signature.

Abutters Pauline and Paul Barrows raised a deeded drainage easement they hold across the property. They also questioned the parking count and sign placement near their driveway sightline. The applicant confirmed a culvert will intercept drainage at its current entry point with a slow-release design. The applicant also said the sign will sit well back of their driveway.
Chair McWilliams praised the traffic study (citing a 1.43% corridor traffic increase, 2016–2022) and the single-access design.
Key Decisions
Approved unanimously by roll call; all eight present, including alternate Lucas Schrage, voted yes. Moved by Kevin Price, seconded by Nancy Litrocapes.
Action Items
None.
26-000404 — Subdivision Amendment — Rock Row South Campus
Discussion Summary

Ian McKim (Jones & Beach Engineers) presented a third amendment. It reconfigures lot lines across several Phase 3 parcels to separate ownership and responsibility under a master condominium/cross-easement agreement.

Staff noted that a November 2025 amendment to this subdivision was never finalized with Portland and was voided. So this amendment builds on the November 2024-approved baseline. Each lot still requires its own site plan review. A site plan is the detailed plan for a building project that the Planning Board reviews.
The board granted a waiver extending the subdivision-plan recording deadline to 150 days (a prior joint-meeting waiver with Portland carries over).
Key Decisions
Approved unanimously by roll call; all eight present, including alternate Lucas Schrage, voted yes. Moved by Nancy Litrocapes, seconded by Lucas Schrage.
Action Items
None.
Workshop — Rock Row Phase 3 Building V, Element Hotel (26-000402)
5-Story, 119-Room Element by Marriott with Ground-Floor Retail
Discussion Summary

Ian McKim introduced Tom Dever and Greg Del Niro of Dever Architects. They presented a 5-story, 119-room Element by Marriott hotel with a ground-floor restaurant/retail. The brand is an extended-stay, sustainability-branded line, and roughly 70% of the units have full kitchens. The site is near Nason's Brook, across Quarry Drive from the garage/residential buildings reviewed at the prior meeting.

The building includes a pass-through “paseo” courtyard. It relies on the adjacent parking garage for guest parking through a planned cross-easement. Proposed facades are aluminum composite panels in gray, white, and wood tones, with ground-floor brick. No public comment.
Board reaction was strongly positive.
Member Jason Frazier asked for more landscape-berming detail and example renderings.
Vice Chair John Turcotte praised the team for showing the building in context with its neighbors for the first time. He asked for similar contextual views going forward.
Member Robin Tannenbaum was at first disoriented by inconsistent plan orientations. Tannenbaum asked for a standard north arrow in future submissions.
Member Karen Axelson confirmed there is no conference/banquet space.

Member Nancy Litrocapes asked how facade consistency would be kept once retail tenants are chosen. The team explained that master developer Waterstone will build out and lease the ground-floor shell directly, using a consistent architectural “frame.”
Key Decisions
No vote — workshop item.
Action Items
None.
Point/Counterpoint — Millbrook Estates: Affordable Housing Need vs. Neighborhood Scale (26-000401)

Tyler Norod (President, Westbrook Development Corporation) reintroduced a project first approved for a contract zone amendment (a special zoning deal for one property) and sketch plan in 2024. It stalled when state funding cycles changed. The design is unchanged.

The proposal is two 36-unit, three-story affordable apartment buildings. They would be funded through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, at 50–60% area median income. They would sit on two vacant lots at the existing 138-unit Millbrook Estates complex. Roughly two-thirds of that complex is already protected open space through a Presumpscot Regional Land Trust partnership.

Norod cited statewide data: roughly 25,000 affordable units needed by 2030, with only 2,000–3,000 built so far. Norod also estimated about 40% of current Westbrook residents income-qualify for this project.
Architects described wraparound porches, gabled (not flat) roofs stepping down toward the rear, and retained street trees intended to soften the buildings' scale.
The critical case
“With the height and placement of these buildings, they want to change the area from suburban to urban... Will Westbrook look back on this and wish it had stayed with the original intent?”

Paulson-Omstead questioned Westbrook Development Corporation's growth pace and motives. Paulson-Omstead also asked whether the original commitments made to the neighborhood about building scale, when Millbrook was first built, had been reviewed. Staff (Rebecca Spitella) responded that roughly 25% of projects approved by this board over the past five to ten years have been affordable housing developments. Staff also confirmed that no zoning change is being requested.
Board reaction — mostly supportive, Chair opposed

Members Karen Axelson and Robin Tannenbaum recused (stepped out of a vote because of a conflict of interest) from this item. Alternate Lucas Schrage was strongly supportive. Schrage called the project “a testament to what you can do” and praised how it fits with the land trust green space.

Vice Chair John Turcotte asked staff to check whether the original Millbrook Estates approval, which came before the current board, set conditions limiting the use of these lots. He also requested more parking buffering.
Member Nancy Litrocapes took a middle position. Litrocapes supported the need in principle but asked how the height gap to smaller homes across the street could be visually bridged.
“I can't imagine a three-story that close to the road with the gable. It'd be one thing if it was a flat roof and not peaking so high, because it's gonna be very towering.”
Key Decisions

No vote — workshop item. The applicant hopes to return with a final application within a couple of months, to keep pace with a Maine Housing funding cycle (application this fall, award decision around November 2026).
Point/Counterpoint — 955 Bridgton Rd.: New Density vs. Existing Drainage & Traffic (26-000403)

Dustin Roma presented a conceptual plan for roughly 10 duplex (condo-for-sale) buildings. They would total 20–26 units (pending formal wetland delineation) on a 10-acre, legally non-conforming parcel (allowed to stay although it no longer meets current zoning). The parcel is reached by a rebuilt private driveway.
The existing home and barn would be demolished. A wooded buffer along the Willow Drive property line would be retained.
The primary open issue is driveway/entrance permitting. Route 302 here is treated as a mobility corridor/arterial inside the City's “urban compact.”

Neighbors turned out in large numbers with overlapping concerns. The central ones were existing drainage problems and Route 302 traffic safety, which long predate this project. Several residents described chronic flooding and water crossing multiple properties via culverts that feed the Millbrook watershed. They described Route 302 as dangerously fast, with a history of collisions and near-misses turning onto or off the road.
“The traffic... Friday nights in the summer, we can't even get out of our road. I've sat there fifteen minutes or so just trying to get out.”
Staff (Rebecca Spitella) gave a long explanation of the process. This is a conceptual workshop stage only. The unit-count range will be fixed once a wetland delineation determines the buildable area.

The word “driveway” refers to legal frontage status (the length of a lot along the street), not literal width. It will be rebuilt to private-way standards with verified emergency-vehicle turning templates.
Staff also said a Westbrook police officer is currently issuing the second-highest number of speeding tickets statewide, in an effort to address Route 302 speeding broadly.

Chair McWilliams asked about buffering options (no fence is permitted under the adjacent homeowners association's covenant). McWilliams also asked about the driveway's raised grade as a possible icy-conditions hazard, and floated a future board site walk. The applicant said he would coordinate the walk with staff once the plan is ready.
Key Decisions
No vote — workshop item.
